pāratantryādyayogācca tena kartāpi kalpitaḥ || 11 || tathāhi sūtrāvataraṇamitthameva karoti tadevam iti | kriyāyāstāvadevamiti kriyāpyarthasya iti tatra tatra sthite iti sūtradvayoktāt sādhakābhāvāt, bādhakayogācca yo'bhāvaḥ nānyo'sti, nānyadasti ityevaṃ sūtradvaye nirdiṣṭaḥ, saṃbandhasyāpi yo'bhāvo'stitvaniścayābhāvanāstitva- niścayarūpaḥ evamiti tatra tatra ityuktena sādhakābhāvena dviṣṭhatvādiyukti- (page 202) bhiśca bādhakena militvā upapāditaḥ, tadidamabhāvacatuṣṭayaṃ militaṃ kartāpi kalpitaḥ ityatra hetutāṃ sūtre tena iti nītam | sā hetutā tu ṭīkāyām abhāvāt iti pañcamyā saṃkṣepāduktā | pañcamī caśabdaṃ ca pūrvasūtreṇa saṃgamayati | saṃbandhaḥ iti nānyo'sti saṃbandho dviṣṭhasyānekatvāt siddhasyānyānapekṣaṇāt pāratantryādiyogācca iti saṃgatiḥ | saṃbandhaḥ ityetāvanmātraṃ tu svakaṇṭhena vivṛtau nirdiṣṭam | dviṣṭhasya iti sāmānyoktāvapi prakaraṇāt saṃbandhasyetyayamapi artho labhyatāmiti | nanu dṛśyānupalapalabdhyaiva nāstitvaniścayakāriṇyā so'rtho bādhyate | vastuta iyameva hi asya bādhā yat niścitanāstitvāvedanaṃ, natu drughaṇena iva śarāvasya viśarārūkaraṇam | sāca atra pradarśitaiva dṛśyasya pramāṇena anupalambhāditi | satyam, anupalabdhyā tu niyatadeśakālāvacchedena nāstitvapratipattiḥ-iha adhunā ghaṭo nāstīti | yadāha -nāsattāniścayo viprakarṣiṇām | iti, yathā iṣṭaṃ viruddhakārye'pi deśakālādyapekṣaṇam | anyathā vyabhicāri syādbhasmevāśītasādhane || iti | tasmāt sārvatrikīṃ saṃbandhāderasattāmāvedayituṃ parābhyupagatatadī- yarūpāsaṃbhavasaṃpādako virodhaḥ prameyaniṣṭho vaktavyaḥ, yat tvayaiva asya rūpamuktaṃ, tat tvaduktenaiva rūpāntareṇa virudhyate iti tata eva tadrūpadvayavirodhasiddhyaiva bādhakābhidhāyī kṛtārtho jāyate iti dūṣaṇahetau na dharmyasiddhyādicodyaprasaṅgaḥ-iti vitatya nirṇītaṃ prasaṅgagranthādāvityāstāṃ tāvat | tatra sāmānyalakṣaṇadvāraṃ bādhakamupanyasyati | yat kila dvayoḥ svarūpasamāptyā yugapat tiṣṭhati, tadekaṃ na bhavati veśmadvayavarti ghaṭadvayamiva | (page 203) ekatvaṃ hi abhinna
**"Thence the agent too is constructed"** The Buddhist's attack has been relentless. He has denied the self, denied the cognition, denied the action. Now he completes it. For what holds all these together — the *relation* between the knower and the known, between the agent and the act — is itself impossible; and once the relation is gone, "thence the agent too is constructed." The agent, like everything else, is only a fabrication, a convenient construction with nothing real behind it. The kārikā's "thence" gathers a fourfold absence as its reason: the absence of the action, the absence of the object, the absence of the relation, and the absence of any determination of being in any of them. And the relation's absence is argued on its own terms. A relation would have to stand *in both* its terms — in the knower and the known at once. But the two-resting thing cannot be one: what stands in two cannot be a single thing, any more than the two jars in the two houses are one jar. Moreover, the established does not expect another — a thing already complete does not reach out for a relation — and the dependence that a relation would impose is itself unfitting. So the relation is absent; and with it, the agent that the relation would bind together is only constructed. Abhinavagupta pauses to make one methodological point, and it is important. The Buddhist thinks he refutes the relation by a bare non-perception — "I do not see it, so it is not." But a bare non-perception proves non-being only within a restriction of place and time: "here, now, there is no jar." It cannot reach the universal non-being of the relation. To do that, one must show a real contradiction in the opponent's own account — that the very form he ascribes to the relation is contradicted by another form he ascribes to it. That is a refutation grounded in the thing itself (prameya-niṣṭha), not a mere failure to perceive. And this is where the pūrvapakṣa — the no-self attack — comes to its close. The Buddhist has shown, to his own satisfaction, that the self, the cognition, the action, and the relation all fall; and "thence the agent too is constructed." The whole edifice of a real knower and doer is, for him, a fabrication. But this is precisely the claim the siddhānta — the established doctrine — will reverse. The Buddhist has built his case on the denial of the real; but his own arguments, turned aright, will show the opposite. The agent is not constructed; the agent is the real, free self — the one who knows and acts, whose cognition and action are not momentary flashes but the ordered operation of a single consciousness. The relation that the Buddhist found impossible is, in truth, the self's own nature — the union of knowledge and action in the one knower. The construction the Buddhist sees is the reality Abhinavagupta will now restore: the self, the Lord, who is not constructed but real. ---

Now it completes itself: > since the relation (between cognition and object, or agent and action) is also impossible, "thence the > agent too is constructed" (kartāpi kalpitaḥ). The "thence" gathers a fourfold absence: the absence of > the action, the absence of the object, the absence of the relation, and the absence of the > determination of the being.
